court: New York Court of General Sessions
holding_summary: Reversing a disorderly-person conviction of a hotel proprietor under Code Crim. Pro. section 899(4), the court held that guilty knowledge is an essential element of that offense and that the fact of legitimate hotel operation is an important consideration in assessing guilt. Because the evidence failed to show the defendant knew prostitutes were resorting to his 250-room hotel, and showed instead an actively managed transient/permanent-guest establishment with screening procedures, the conviction could not stand.

quotes.text: That the defendant was actually maintaining a hotel was established by the evidence.

A hotel, no matter how large, costly or elegant its furnishings, may be a bawdy house, or house for the resort of prostitutes, and kept as such by the proprietor, in whole or in part; but in determining the guilt of a defendant charged with being a disorderly person the fact that the premises are actually maintained as a hotel and the legal obligations of the defendant in maintaining them as such may be an important consideration.
On the facts shown in this case, the court cannot sustain the judgment of conviction; the guilt of the defendant has not been established beyond a reasonable doubt.

notes: Adverse-embed selector fired on regulation language, but the substantive holding protects the commercial lodging operator (hotel keeper) from strict liability absent guilty knowledge.

holding_summary: A licensed hotel keeper with thirty-two furnished rooms for lodgers sued a police captain who stationed officers at the hotel and had them tell prospective customers the place was a disorderly house likely to be raided. The court held police officers may lawfully station themselves at and inspect a liquor-licensed hotel, but enjoined the captain from making unproven statements to customers characterizing it as disorderly and threatening raids, since such conduct proceeded without warrant of law and threatened the plaintiff's lawful business.

quotes.text: said premises contain thirty-two furnished-rooms for lodgers, a restaurant and a bar

There seems, therefore, to be abundant authority in the statutes and the cases for the captain of police taking such action as his discretion warrants for posting his officers and making his inspections.
So far, then, as he and his officers interfered with the customers of this place by statements as to its character and threats of possible raids, he proceeds, in my judgment, without warrant of law.

The motion will be denied so far as it seeks to obtain an injunction preventing the posting of officers and inspection of the premises, and granted so far as it relates to the interference with proposed customers by volunteered .statements and threats.

notes: Mixed: sustains police inspection power over a licensed lodging house (adverse) while protecting the lawful lodging/hotel business from unwarranted deterrence of customers (favorable).
